triples.relationship: fasting joined to turning toward God
triples.rationale: Nineveh's people respond to the divine warning with belief, fasting and sackcloth. Joel calls for turning to the Lord with fasting and wholehearted repentance, connecting the outward fast with the response to God.
triples.source_text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

triples.relationship: parallel royal humbling after a prophetic warning
triples.rationale: Nineveh's king leaves his throne and royal clothing and puts on sackcloth upon hearing the message. Ahab likewise responds to the prophetic word by weeping, tearing his tunic, wearing sackcloth and fasting, after which the Lord acknowledges his humbling.
triples.source_text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.

target_units.text: Because of the word, Ahab was stricken before the Lord: he went about weeping, tore his tunic, tied sackcloth around his body, fasted, and put on sackcloth on the day he struck Naboth the Jezreelite.
The Lord’s word came through His servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said,
“Have you seen how Ahab has been stricken before Me? I will not bring the harm in his days, but in his son’s days I will bring the harm.”

triples.relationship: parallel communal abstention from food and drink
triples.rationale: Nineveh's royal decree forbids food and water for the people and livestock. Esther similarly commands the gathered Jews in Susa to fast without eating or drinking. The shared feature is a publicly directed fast with both food and drink withheld; Nineveh's decree additionally includes livestock.
triples.source_text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”

target_units.text: “Go, assemble the Jews in Susa, and all of you fast for me. Neither eat nor drink for three days, night and day; I and my maids will also go without food. Then I will enter the king’s presence contrary to the law, even if I must perish.”

triples.relationship: fasting accompanied by rejection of injustice
triples.rationale: Nineveh's decree joins sackcloth and crying to God with each person turning from evil and the injustice in their hands. Isaiah likewise says that sackcloth and outward fasting are inadequate and calls instead for releasing people from injustice and caring for the vulnerable.
triples.source_text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:

target_units.text: I did not choose this fast, or a day for a person to humble his life. Even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, you will not thereby call it an acceptable fast.

‘It is not such a fast that I chose,’ says the Lord. ‘Instead, loosen every bond of injustice, undo the strangling ties of coercive agreements, release the crushed, and tear up every unjust written contract.
Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

triples.relationship: shared hope that God may relent
triples.rationale: Nineveh's decree asks who knows whether God will relent and turn from wrath so they do not perish. Joel likewise asks who knows whether He will turn and relent, expressing hope rather than assuming the outcome.
triples.source_text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”

target_units.text: Who knows whether He will turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him, a sacrifice and drink offering for the Lord our God?

triples.rationale: God sees Nineveh turn from evil and does not bring the announced calamity. Jeremiah explicitly states that when a threatened nation turns from its evils, the Lord will change His mind concerning the destruction He planned.
triples.source_text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

target_units.text: At last I will speak concerning a nation or kingdom, to remove them and destroy,
and if that nation turns from all their evils, I will change My mind concerning the evils I planned to do to them.

triples.relationship: narrative analogy of resentment at mercy
triples.rationale: Jonah is grieved after Nineveh is spared, and his following prayer names God's mercy as the issue. The older son likewise objects when his father welcomes the returning son, and the father explains why restoration calls for joy. The relationship is a shared response of resentment at mercy extended to another.
triples.source_text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.

target_units.text: But he became angry and was unwilling to enter. His father came out and pleaded with him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, all these years I have served you as a slave, and I never disobeyed your command; yet you never gave me a young goat so that I might be glad with my friends.
But when this son of yours came, who devoured your livelihood with prostitutes, you slaughtered the fattened calf for him!’
And he said to him, ‘Child, you are always with me, and everything of mine is yours.
But we had to be glad and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found.’”

triples.relationship: shared declaration of God's merciful character
triples.rationale: Jonah describes God as merciful, compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy when explaining his flight. Exodus's proclamation of the Lord's name uses the same cluster of merciful attributes.
triples.source_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

triples.rationale: Jonah explains that he knew God was merciful, compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy and one who relents concerning calamities. Joel uses that same sequence of attributes to ground the appeal to turn to the Lord.
triples.source_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

target_units.text: Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

triples.rationale: Jonah asks the Lord to take his life because death seems better to him. Elijah likewise asks the Lord to take his life during his distressed withdrawal, giving a close parallel between the two prophets' death wishes.
triples.source_text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”

target_units.text: He himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, came, and sat under a single broom bush. He asked that his life might end and said, “Let it be enough now! I pray Thee, take my life from me, Lord, for I am no better than my fathers.”

triples.rationale: The Lord first asks whether Jonah is deeply grieved after Nineveh is spared. The question recurs with the gourd named explicitly in verse 9, drawing Jonah's reaction to the city and his reaction to the plant into comparison.
triples.source_text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

target_units.text: God said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved about the gourd?” He said, “I am deeply grieved, even to death.”

triples.rationale: God provides the gourd to shade Jonah's head and shelter him. The psalm describes the Lord as a shelter and promises that the sun will not scorch the one He guards, corresponding to the protection the plant gives before its removal.
triples.source_text: The Lord God commanded a gourd, and it grew up above Jonah’s head, to provide shade over his head and shelter him from his troubles. Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great joy.

target_units.text: The Lord will guard you; the Lord is your shelter at your right hand.
By day the sun will not scorch you, nor the moon by night.

triples.rationale: God commands a worm that strikes Jonah's protective gourd. Earlier He commanded the sea creature to swallow Jonah. Both episodes show a creature changing the prophet's circumstances under divine command, within the book's larger contrast with Jonah's initial flight from his own command.
triples.source_text: God commanded a worm at dawn the next day; it struck the gourd, and it dried up.

target_units.text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

triples.relationship: same-book motif of divinely sent winds
triples.rationale: God commands a scorching wind that contributes to Jonah's distress on land. Earlier the Lord raised the great wind that endangered his sea journey; the two episodes place the prophet under winds directed by God in different settings.
triples.source_text: As the sun rose, God commanded a burning, scorching wind. The sun struck Jonah’s head; he lost heart, renounced his life and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

target_units.text: The Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great surge on the sea; the ship was in danger of being shattered.

triples.rationale: The Lord asks about Jonah's deep grief over the gourd, repeating the earlier question after the city's deliverance. The repetition prepares the comparison between the plant Jonah values and Nineveh's people and livestock.
triples.source_text: God said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved about the gourd?” He said, “I am deeply grieved, even to death.”

target_units.text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

triples.rationale: The Lord points to Jonah sparing a brief-lived gourd for which he had not labored. The next question applies that concern to the far greater case of Nineveh with its many people and livestock, completing the argument about compassion.
triples.source_text: The Lord said, “You spared the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.

target_units.text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

triples.relationship: divine compassion extending across God's works
triples.rationale: The Lord's question includes both Nineveh's numerous people and its livestock in the reason for sparing the city. The psalm describes the Lord as merciful and His compassions as extending over all His works, corresponding to the breadth of that concern.
triples.source_text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

target_units.text: Compassionate and merciful is the Lord, patient and abundant in mercy.
The Lord is kind to all, and His compassions are over all His works.

triples.relationship: parallel divine questions about sparing a people
triples.rationale: The Lord asks whether He should not spare Nineveh. Hosea similarly presents God's questions about how to deal with Ephraim and His refusal to act according to furious anger or erase them. The populations differ, but both speeches make divine compassion central to withholding destruction.
triples.source_text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

target_units.text: How shall I deal with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel? How shall I deal with you? Shall I make you like Adama and like Seboim? My heart turned within itself; My change of mind was stirred together.
I will certainly not act according to My furious anger; I will certainly not abandon Ephraim to be erased. For I am God and not a human being, holy within you, and I will not enter a city.
